catalog_quote: Basically, the primary stress in any word falls on the first syllable, with secondary stress on the third syllable of a four-syllable root or a trisyllabic word carrying a monosyllabic suffix and/or on the first syllable of any bound disyllabic morpheme, or on the first of a pair of bound monosyllabic morphemes if it does not tend to form a diphthong or long vowel with the preceding vowel (i.e. is not -yi after /a/ or /i/). A non-productive stem formative (like -lu in parrkulu 'two') is not treated as a bound morpheme but as part of the root. Secondary stresses are not always detectable. ... An alternative for words like the last example above, with a monosyllabic suffix preceding a disyllabic, is to have the secondary stress on the monosyllabic suffix ... the only other vowel-initial bound morpheme, the emphatic marker -ardi, is stressed on its first syllable and often even carries the…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed initial primary stress, weight-blind; morphologically conditioned secondary stress; listed lexical/morphological exceptions such as -ardi and distorted final vowels; phrase stress separate) rests on the standard and only reference grammar of the language, Breen 2004 (PL 558), sec. 3.6, and every deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim on the page image we hold (p.30) and held scanned text (p.31, p.33). Glottolog lists nothing better (the other items are a duplicate record, an unpublished Breen ms absorbed into the grammar, an unpublished Nhirrpi dialect sketch, and 19th-c./missionary sketches); Crossref and lingbuzz show no phonology/prosody study; the language is extinct so no instrumental work is expected. Only nit: the locator should read printed pp.30-33 (3.6.1 Phrase stress starts on p.33), not pp.30-32. no reclassification, no upgrade needed (grade is already page-image)
